597059.old: Most of these organizations also recommend decreasing the total amount of fat in the diet.

Recently, certain fats called trans fats have been implicated in the presence of heart disease. These are fats from animal sources and are also produced when liquid oils are exposed to partial hydrogenation, an industrial process that increases their saturation. Trans fats are used in many prepared and fried foods. Because they bring with them the health risks that naturally occurring saturated fats do, there has been some effort to better quantify the presence of trans fats in food products. <abbr title="United States">US</abbr> law now requires that food labels list the amount of trans fat in each serving.
597059.new: Trans fats are also linked to heart disease. Small amounts occur naturally in meat and dairy foods, but most of the trans fat in the American diet once came from partially hydrogenated oils. These were made by partial hydrogenation, an industrial process that adds hydrogen to some of the C=C double bonds of a liquid oil (Sections 3.2 and 3.4). Trans fats raise LDL (“bad”) cholesterol and lower HDL (“good”) cholesterol, so they are even worse for the heart than saturated fats. <abbr title="United States">US</abbr> food labels list the amount of trans fat in each serving, and the <abbr title="Food and Drug Administration">FDA</abbr> has removed partially hydrogenated oils from the U.S. food supply.

597093.old: The main reason for methanol’s toxicity is that we have liver enzymes that catalyze its oxidation to formaldehyde, the simplest member of the
597093.new: Methanol itself is only mildly toxic; the danger comes from what liver enzymes make from it. They first oxidize it to formaldehyde, the simplest member of the

597093.old: Formaldehyde reacts rapidly with the components of cells, coagulating proteins in much the same way that cooking coagulates an egg. This property of formaldehyde accounts for much of the toxicity of methanol.
597093.new: The formaldehyde is quickly oxidized further to formic acid, which is present in the body as the formate ion. Formate is the main poison: it causes metabolic acidosis (blood pH below normal) and damages the optic nerve, which is why methanol can cause blindness. The first-line antidote is fomepizole, a drug that blocks alcohol dehydrogenase so that methanol is not converted to these products; ethanol was the older alternative (Section 4.5).

597105.old: Methanal produced by the oxidation of methanol is a poisonous substance that damages many tissues and causes blindness.
597105.new: Methanol is oxidized to methanal (formaldehyde) and then to formic acid. Formic acid, present in the body as formate, is the main poison: it causes metabolic acidosis and damages the optic nerve, which can cause blindness.

597105.old: In cases of methanol poisoning, ethanol is injected intravenously into the patient to compete with methanol for alcohol dehydrogenase enzyme. This way, methanol is excreted before converting to poisonous methanal in the body.
597105.new: In methanol poisoning, the first-line antidote is fomepizole, a drug that blocks alcohol dehydrogenase. Ethanol, which competes with methanol for the same enzyme, was the older alternative. Either way, methanol is excreted unchanged before it can be converted to its toxic products.

597127.old: Amide bonds in drugs survive stomach acid for the hour or two they spend there and are broken down later, mainly in the liver, which is why amide drugs such as acetaminophen survive the stomach when given by mouth and why amide anesthetics such as lidocaine last longer than ester anesthetics. Ester drugs, by contrast, are attacked quickly by esterases in plasma. Liver disease slows amide hydrolysis, so a patient's liver enzymes (ALT/AST) matter when these drugs are dosed; that judgment belongs to the prescriber, but the chemistry behind it is this section.
597127.new: Amide bonds survive the hour or two a drug spends in stomach acid, which is one reason amide drugs such as acetaminophen can be given by mouth. Amide drugs are then cleared mainly by enzymes in the liver, and not always by cutting the amide bond: acetaminophen is mostly cleared by attaching a glucuronide or sulfate group to its phenol OH, and lidocaine is broken down by liver enzymes. Ester drugs, by contrast, are hydrolyzed quickly by esterases in plasma. Liver disease slows the metabolism of amide drugs, so a patient's liver function matters when these drugs are dosed; that judgment belongs to the prescriber.

597163.old: Prions are small proteins found in nerve tissue. Their exact functions are unknown, but when they misfold, they can cause more normal proteins to misfold. This protein misfolding is related to diseases such as mad cow disease in cows, Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease in humans, Alzheimer's disease, and familial amyloid cardiomyopathy or polyneuropathy, as well as intracellular aggregation diseases such as Huntington's and Parkinson's disease.
597163.new:
Prions are misfolded forms of a normal protein found in nerve tissue (the prion protein). A misfolded prion can make normal copies of the same protein misfold too, so the damage spreads. Prions cause mad cow disease in cattle and Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (CJD) in humans.

Other diseases also involve misfolded proteins that clump together, but they are not prion diseases. Examples are Alzheimer's disease (β-amyloid plaques), Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, and familial amyloid cardiomyopathy or polyneuropathy.

597163.old: the misfolded form is rich in sticky β-sheet, it converts normal copies into the same shape, and the aggregates survive the heat of ordinary sterilization.
597163.new: the misfolded form is rich in sticky β-sheet and clumps together. Prions go further: a prion converts normal copies of its protein into the same shape, and prion aggregates survive the heat of ordinary sterilization.

597169.old: Chemotherapy is the strategic use of chemicals (that is, drugs) to destroy infectious microorganisms or cancer cells without causing excessive damage to the other, healthy cells of the host. From bacteria to humans, the metabolic pathways of all living organisms are quite similar, so the search for safe and effective chemotherapeutic agents is a formidable task. Many well-established chemotherapeutic drugs function by inhibiting a critical enzyme in the cells of the invading organism.
597169.new: An antibiotic is a drug that kills bacteria or stops their growth. Many antibiotics work by inhibiting an enzyme that bacteria need but human cells do not have, so the drug harms the bacteria and leaves the patient’s own cells alone.

597169.old: An antibiotic is a compound that kills bacteria; it may come from a natural source such as molds or be synthesized with a structure analogous to a naturally occurring antibacterial compound. Antibiotics constitute no well-defined class of chemically related substances, but many of them work by effectively inhibiting a variety of enzymes essential to bacterial growth.

Penicillin, one of the most widely used antibiotics in the world, was fortuitously discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928, when he noticed antibacterial properties in a mold growing on a bacterial culture plate. In 1938, Ernst Chain and Howard Florey began an intensive effort to isolate penicillin from the mold and study its properties. The large quantities of penicillin needed for this research became available through development of a corn-based nutrient medium that the mold loved and through the discovery of a higher-yielding strain of mold at a United States Department of Agriculture research center near Peoria, Illinois. Even so, it was not until 1944 that large quantities of penicillin were being produced and made available for the treatment of bacterial infections.
597169.new: Penicillin was discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928, in a mold growing on a bacterial culture plate. It became the first antibiotic produced in large amounts, in the 1940s.

597169.old: Penicillin functions by interfering with the synthesis of cell walls of reproducing bacteria. It does so by inhibiting an enzyme—transpeptidase—that catalyzes the last step in bacterial cell-wall biosynthesis. The defective walls cause bacterial cells to burst. Human cells are not affected because they have cell membranes, not cell walls.
597169.new: Penicillin blocks the bacterial enzymes (transpeptidases) that cross-link the cell wall. The enzyme becomes covalently bonded to the drug, so penicillin is a good example of an irreversible inhibitor. With a weak wall, the bacterial cell bursts. Human cells have no cell wall and no transpeptidase, so they are not affected.

597169.old: Several naturally occurring penicillins have been isolated. They are distinguished by different R groups connected to a common structure: a four-member cyclic amide (called a lactam ring) fused to a five-member ring. The addition of appropriate organic compounds to the culture medium leads to the production of the different kinds of penicillin.
597169.new: All penicillins share a β-lactam ring, a strained four-membered cyclic amide fused to a five-membered ring; they differ only in the R group (structures below). The cephalosporins are related β-lactam antibiotics.

597169.old: The penicillins are effective against gram-positive bacteria (bacteria capable of being stained by Gram’s stain) and a few gram-negative bacteria (including the intestinal bacterium Escherichia coli). They are effective in the treatment of diphtheria, gonorrhea, pneumonia, syphilis, many pus infections, and certain types of boils. Penicillin G was the earliest penicillin to be used on a wide scale. However, it cannot be administered orally because it is quite unstable; the acidic pH of the stomach converts it to an inactive derivative. The major oral penicillins—penicillin V, ampicillin, and amoxicillin—on the other hand, are acid stable.
597169.new:
Penicillins work best against Gram-positive bacteria, which have a thick peptidoglycan cell wall and stain purple with Gram’s stain; some, such as amoxicillin, also act on certain Gram-negative bacteria. Penicillin G is destroyed by stomach acid and is given by injection; penicillin V, ampicillin and amoxicillin are acid-stable and are taken by mouth.

Resistance. Some bacteria make β-lactamase (penicillinase), an enzyme that hydrolyzes the amide in the β-lactam ring and destroys the drug. Others, such as methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), change the target enzyme so the drug no longer binds. Every unneeded antibiotic dose favors resistant bacteria, which is why hospitals and clinics practice antibiotic stewardship: the right drug, at the right dose, only when it is needed.

Allergy. A true penicillin allergy can cause anaphylaxis, a life-threatening reaction, so the allergy history is checked before every dose. However, most people whose charts say “penicillin allergy” turn out not to be allergic when they are tested, and an allergy evaluation can let them receive the most effective drug.

597169.old: Some strains of bacteria become resistant to penicillin through a mutation that allows them to synthesize an enzyme—penicillinase—that breaks the antibiotic down (by cleavage of the amide linkage in the lactam ring). To combat these strains, scientists have synthesized penicillin analogs (such as methicillin) that are not inactivated by penicillinase.

Some people (perhaps 5% of the population) are allergic to penicillin and therefore must be treated with other antibiotics. Their allergic reaction can be so severe that a fatal coma may occur if penicillin is inadvertently administered to them. Fortunately, several other antibiotics have been discovered. Most, including aureomycin and streptomycin, are the products of microbial synthesis. Others, such as the semisynthetic penicillins and tetracyclines, are made by chemical modifications of antibiotics; and some, like chloramphenicol, are manufactured entirely by chemical synthesis. They are as effective as penicillin in destroying infectious microorganisms. Many of these antibiotics exert their effects by blocking protein synthesis in microorganisms.

Initially, antibiotics were considered miracle drugs, substantially reducing the number of deaths from blood poisoning, pneumonia, and other infectious diseases. Some seven decades ago, a person with a major infection almost always died. Today, such deaths are rare. Seven decades ago, pneumonia was a dreaded killer of people of all ages. Today, it kills only the very old or those ill from other causes. Antibiotics have indeed worked miracles in our time, but even miracle drugs have limitations. Not long after the drugs were first used, disease organisms began to develop strains resistant to them. In a race to stay ahead of resistant bacterial strains, scientists continue to seek new antibiotics. The penicillins have now been partially displaced by related compounds, such as the cephalosporins and vancomycin. Unfortunately, some strains of bacteria have already shown resistance to these antibiotics.

597192.old: There are two types of diabetes. In immune-mediated diabetes, insufficient amounts of insulin are produced. This type of diabetes develops early in life and is also known as Type 1 diabetes, as well as insulin-dependent or juvenile-onset diabetes. Symptoms are rapidly reversed by the administration of insulin, and Type 1 diabetics can lead active lives provided they receive insulin as needed. Because insulin is a protein that is readily digested in the small intestine, it cannot be taken orally and must be injected at least once a day.
597192.new: There are two main types of diabetes. In type 1 diabetes, the body’s immune system destroys the insulin-making β cells of the pancreas, so little or no insulin is made. It is most often found in children and young adults, but it can start at any age. People with type 1 diabetes need insulin every day for life, given by injection or by an insulin pump. Insulin is a protein, so it would be digested in the stomach and small intestine if it were swallowed.

597192.old: In Type 1 diabetes, insulin-producing cells of the pancreas are destroyed by the body’s immune system. Researchers are still trying to find out why. Meanwhile, they have developed a simple blood test capable of predicting who will develop Type 1 diabetes several years before the disease becomes apparent. The blood test reveals the presence of antibodies that destroy the body’s insulin-producing cells.
597192.new: A blood test for the antibodies that attack the β cells can show who is at high risk of type 1 diabetes, sometimes years before symptoms begin.

597192.old: Type 2 diabetes, also known as noninsulin-dependent or adult-onset diabetes, is by far the more common, representing about 95% of diagnosed diabetic cases. (Current CDC estimates are about 38 million Americans with diabetes, 90–95% of them type 2; see Section 13.8.) Type 2 diabetics usually produce sufficient amounts of insulin, but either the insulin-producing cells in the pancreas do not release enough of it, or it is not used properly because of defective insulin receptors or a lack of insulin receptors on the target cells. In many of these people, the disease can be controlled with a combination of diet and exercise alone. For some people who are overweight, losing weight is sufficient to bring their blood sugar level into the normal range, after which medication is not required if they exercise regularly and eat wisely.
597192.new: Type 2 diabetes is by far the more common type: about 90–95% of people with diabetes have type 2. (Current CDC estimates are about 38 million Americans with diabetes; Section 13.7 gives the figures for Valley counties.) In type 2 diabetes the body still makes insulin, but muscle, fat, and liver cells respond poorly to it (insulin resistance), and over time the pancreas cannot make enough extra insulin to keep up. It usually develops slowly in adults, but it is now also seen in teenagers and children. Healthy eating, regular physical activity, and weight loss (for people who are overweight) lower blood glucose, and for some people they are enough on their own.

597192.old: Those who require medication may use oral antidiabetic drugs that stimulate the islet cells to secrete insulin. First-generation antidiabetic drugs stimulated the release of insulin. Newer second-generation drugs, such as glyburide, do as well, but they also increase the sensitivity of cell receptors to insulin. Some individuals with Type 2 diabetes do not produce enough insulin and thus do not respond to these oral medications; they must use insulin. In both Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes, the blood sugar level must be carefully monitored and adjustments made in diet or medication to keep the level as normal as possible (70–120 mg/dL).
597192.new: Many people with type 2 diabetes also take medicine. Metformin, usually the first drug used, lowers the amount of glucose the liver releases and helps cells respond better to insulin (Section 13.9). Sulfonylureas, such as glyburide (shown above), make the pancreas release more insulin; because they push insulin out even when the person has not eaten, they can cause low blood glucose. GLP-1 receptor agonists (for example, semaglutide) increase insulin release after meals, slow stomach emptying, and reduce appetite. SGLT2 inhibitors make the kidneys excrete more glucose in the urine. Many people with type 2 diabetes eventually need insulin as well. In every type of diabetes, blood glucose is checked often and diet and medicine are adjusted to keep it as close to normal as is safe. A normal fasting blood glucose is 70–99 mg/dL (Section 13.7).

597193.old: The accumulation of lactate makes muscles tire and sore.
597193.new: During hard exercise, lactate and H<sup>+</sup> build up in the muscle. The H<sup>+</sup>, not the lactate, contributes to the burning feeling and fatigue; lactate itself is a fuel, not a poison (Section 13.4). The soreness felt a day or two later comes from small injuries to the muscle fibers, not from lactate.

597202.old: Recall that \(\ce{C=O}\) is stronger bond (~800 kJ/mol bond dissociation energy) compared to \(\ce{C=C}\) bond (~600 kJ/mole bond dissociation energy). \(\ce{NADH}\) is more energetic than \(\ce{FADH2}\). Therefore, any oxidation reaction involving carbonyl (\(\ce{C=O}\)) group produces \(\ce{NADH}\) and any oxidation involving \(\ce{C=C}\) bond produces \(\ce{FADH2}\).
597202.new: The rule is empirical: an oxidation that turns an alcohol into a carbonyl (\(\ce{C=O}\)) group produces \(\ce{NADH}\), and an oxidation that turns a \(\ce{C-C}\) single bond into a \(\ce{C=C}\) double bond produces \(\ce{FADH2}\). \(\ce{NADH}\) is worth more ATP than \(\ce{FADH2}\) (2.5 versus 1.5, Section 14.4).
